procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 29, 1966 of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 104 of 1966, which affirmed the trial court's conviction of Munney Khan for murder under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Madhya Pradesh High Court dismissed Munney Khan's appeal summarily, agreeing generally with the conclusions of the trial court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Munney Khan appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's decision.

decision.conviction_status: The conviction under s. 302, l.P.C., is set aside, and the appellant is convicted instead under the first part of section 304, I.P.C.
decision.sentence_status: The sentence of imprisonment for life is set aside and, instead, a sentence of seven years' rigorous imprisonment is awarded.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant for the offence under s. 302, I.P.C. is justified.

facts: The deceased, Reotisingh, had overpowered the appellant's brother, Zulfiquar, during a quarrel.
The deceased was sitting on the brother's chest and hitting him with his fists.
In response, the appellant stabbed the deceased in the back with a knife.
These facts were established by the trial court, affirmed by the High Court, and were not disputed before the Supreme Court.
law: The court considered the right of private defense, which allows a person to use force to protect another from harm.
If a person exceeds the right of private defense, their act, which might otherwise be considered murder, is reduced to the lesser offense of culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
This offense is punishable under the first part of section 304 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.).
application: The Court acknowledged that the appellant had a right of private defense to protect his brother from the assault.
However, the Court found that the appellant exceeded this right by using a knife against the deceased, who was unarmed and only using his fists.
The use of a deadly weapon was deemed disproportionate to the threat posed by the deceased.

Because the appellant used excessive force and exceeded his right of private defense, his crime was determined not to be murder under s. 302, I.P.C., but rather culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s. 304, I.P.C.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction for murder under s. 302, I.P.C. was not justified. It held that the appellant had exceeded his right of private defense and was guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Consequently, the Court set aside the murder conviction, convicted the appellant under the first part of s. 304, I.P.C., and reduced his sentence from life imprisonment to seven years' rigorous imprisonment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant had exceeded his right of private defence, making him guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s. 304, I.P.C.

facts: The deceased (Reotisingh) picked a quarrel with the appellant's brother (Zulfiquar).
The deceased overpowered the appellant's brother, threw him on the ground, sat on his chest, and was hitting him with his fists.
In response, the appellant stabbed the deceased in the back with a knife, causing a fatal injury.
law: A person has a right of private defence to protect another person's body from an offence.
This right is governed by Section 101 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.), which is subject to two limitations:
1. The force used must not exceed the minimum required for the defence.
2. In exercising this right, one cannot cause death unless the assault is of a very serious nature (as specified in s. 100 I.P.C.).
If a person exceeds the right of private defence and causes death, the offence is culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under Section 304, I.P.C.
application: The Court first established that a right of private defence had accrued to the appellant because his brother was being assaulted by the deceased, who was the aggressor.
However, the Court found this right to be limited. The threat posed by the deceased was only fist blows, which did not justify a fatal response.
The Court reasoned that the appellant's action of using a knife was itself in excess of the right of private defence against fist blows.
This excess became "much more excessive" when the appellant used the knife to inflict a blow on a vital part of the deceased's body (the back), an act which was likely to cause death.

The Court concluded that while the appellant's intent to cause a fatal injury would normally constitute murder, the fact that he was acting in the exercise of a right of private defence (even though he exceeded it) brought the case under an exception.
Therefore, the act was not murder, but culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the appellant had exceeded his right of private defence. The force used (a fatal knife stab) was disproportionate to the threat (fist blows). Consequently, the Court found him guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under the first part of s. 304, I.P.C., rather than murder under s. 302, I.P.C.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant for the offence under s. 302, I.P.C. is justified.
appellant_arguments: The conviction for murder under s. 302, I.P.C. was not justified because the appellant was exercising his right of private defence to protect his brother.
The facts established that the deceased was the aggressor who had picked a quarrel, overpowered the appellant's brother, and was beating him with fists.
respondent_arguments: The conviction for murder under s. 302, I.P.C. was justified, as affirmed by the High Court.
The prosecution's initial case was that the appellant and his brother had launched the attack, which would negate any right of private defence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant had exceeded his right of private defence, making him guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s. 304, I.P.C.
appellant_arguments: As an alternative to the murder charge, the appellant argued that even if he exceeded his right of private defence, the offence should be reduced from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s. 304, I.P.C.
respondent_arguments: The appellant's act of using a knife against an unarmed man constituted murder under s. 302, I.P.C., and was not merely a case of exceeding the right of private defence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a person, in the legitimate exercise of the right of private defense of another's body, exceeds that right by using more force than is necessary and causes death, the offense is culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under the first part of section 304, I.P.C., and not murder under section 302, I.P.C.
obiter: In a free fight, it is dangerous as a general rule to grant a right of private defense to either party or their sympathizers.
If there is no initial right of private defence then there can hardly be any question of exceeding that right.
The right of private defense is essentially a defensive right circumscribed by the statute, and should not be allowed as a pretext for vindictive, aggressive or retributive action.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On the facts as found, the deceased was the aggressor, which gave the appellant a right of private defence of the body of his brother. However, the appellant exceeded that right. The use of a knife against an unarmed man was in itself excessive, and became much more so when the blow was delivered to a vital part of the body. While the existence of the right of private defence prevents a conviction for murder, the act of exceeding that right by intentionally causing a fatal injury constitutes the offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under the first part of section 304, I.P.C.
legal_tests_applied: The right of private defence is governed by s. 101, I.P.C., and is subject to the limitations that in the exercise of the right death may not be caused, and that the force used should not exceed the minimum required to save the person in whose defence it is used.
If a person causes death in the exercise of the right of private defence, but exceeds that right, the case falls under the exception under which culpable homicide does not amount to murder.

Where a blow is given in the back with a knife, an inference follows that the appellant intended to cause death or at least intended to cause such injury as would, in the ordinary course of nature, result in his death.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant exceeded his right of private defence because the use of the knife itself was in excess of the right, and it became much more excessive when the blow was given in a vital part of the victim's body and was, in the ordinary course of nature, likely to cause his death.

The court inferred from the nature of the attack—a knife blow to the back—that the appellant intended to cause death or a fatal injury, which is a necessary element for a conviction under the first part of s. 304, I.P.C.
why_respondent_won: The respondent secured a conviction for culpable homicide because the court found that while a right of private defence existed, the appellant's act of using a knife and stabbing the deceased in a vital part of the body was a clear case of exceeding that right.

The court concluded that the appellant's actions would have constituted murder had there been no right of private defence at all, thus justifying a conviction for the lesser but related offence under s. 304, I.P.C.
policy_considerations: The right of private defence is essentially a defensive right circumscribed by the statute, and should not be allowed as a pretext for vindictive, aggressive or retributive purpose.
When two parties are having a free fight... it is dangerous as a general rule to clothe either of them or his sympathiscr with a right of private defence.

Courts should be careful in seeing that no one on the mere pretext of exercise of right of private defence take, sides in a quarrel between two or more persons and inflicts injuries on one or the other.
There is also no right of private defence when there is time to have recourse to the protection of public authorities.
